also: not to mention the fact that

terms.gloss: not to mention, to say nothing of
terms.grammar: purpose clause standing outside the sentence; ut omittam with the accusative, or with quod and the indicative
evidence: Cic. Brut. 266: ut omittam cētera quae sunt innumerābilia (Lewis & Short s.v. omittō)
Cic. Cat. 3.18: ut omittam cētera (Lewis & Short s.v. cēterus)
terms.comment: “That I may pass over”: the orator’s way of naming a thing while saying he will not dwell on it. The same verb in the indicative, omittō, “I say nothing of”, opens a list of things passed over.

evidence: Cic. Mur. 15: mittō proelia, praetereō oppugnātiōnēs oppidōrum (Lewis & Short s.v. mittō)
Traupman 103: not to mention the fact that, ut mittam quod (+ indic.)
terms.comment: Mittō, like omittō, means “pass over” in speaking; “not to mention the fact that” is ut mittam quod with the indicative.

evidence: Traupman 103: not to mention, ut nōn (or nihil) dīcam dē (+ abl.)
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase; not quoted in Lewis & Short. Beware nē dīcam, which is something else: “not to say”, “I might almost say”, softening a stronger word (crūdēlem Castorem, nē dīcam scelerātum, Cic. Deiot. 2, Lewis & Short s.v. crūdēlis).

sources: Lewis & Short: omitto · Lewis & Short: mitto
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 103, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
